purpose: Levoleucovorin is used alongside or after certain cancer chemotherapy drugs, especially methotrexate, to protect your healthy cells from being damaged. It is also used to help treat a type of colorectal cancer when combined with other chemotherapy medicines. Think of it as a 'rescue' medicine that shields your body from some of the harmful effects of strong cancer drugs.
how_it_works: Methotrexate and similar drugs work by blocking folate, a B-vitamin your cells need to grow and survive — this helps kill cancer cells, but it can also hurt healthy cells. Levoleucovorin steps in and provides a usable form of folate that healthy cells can absorb and use, essentially rescuing them. Cancer cells are less able to use this rescue agent, so your normal cells get protection while the cancer drug still does its job.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, mouth sores, diarrhea, stomach pain, and fatigue are the most common side effects. Some people may notice skin rash or itching. These effects are often related to the chemotherapy being used alongside it.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have ever had an allergic reaction to leucovorin or folic acid. If you are taking methotrexate, it is very important to take levoleucovorin exactly on schedule — missing or delaying doses can be dangerous. Let your doctor know about all your medications, especially seizure medicines like phenobarbital or phenytoin, as levoleucovorin can affect how they work. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
typical_dosing: Dosing is carefully calculated by your doctor or pharmacist based on your body size and the chemotherapy you are receiving. It is usually given by injection or IV infusion in a clinic or hospital setting. Timing is very important — it is often given at specific hours after methotrexate to work properly. Always follow your healthcare team's exact schedule.
